8.4. Euler, Symmetry, and Boussinesq Flow🔗

8.4.1. Incompressible Euler Flow🔗

Removing viscosity from the momentum law leaves the incompressible Euler equations:

\partial_tu+(u\mathbin\cdot\nabla)u+\nabla p=f, \qquad \nabla\mathbin\cdot u=0.

The equation describes an ideal fluid with no viscous dissipation. Its nonlinearity is the vector analogue of Burgers self-transport, while pressure couples all components through incompressibility.

Initial-value data consist of a force f, a prescribed velocity u_0, and distributional incompressibility of u_0. A finite-time residual solution stores u, p, a positive horizon T, the Euler momentum equation and pointwise incompressibility on (0,T)\times\mathbb R^n, and the exact value u(0,x)=u_0(x).

A residual solution carries no differentiability. A smooth solution also requires ambient smoothness at every positive-time point and one-sided continuity of velocity at t=0. A global smooth solution has these properties at all positive times and relative smoothness on [0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^n. Every global smooth solution restricts, with the same fields and data, to every positive finite horizon. Smoothness alone on the whole space does not imply the L^2 bounds, decay, and spacetime integrability required by a weak solution, so a smooth solution is weak only once those bounds are proved.

uses 0

Every time derivative, convective term, pressure gradient, and divergence is zero. Constant zero fields are smooth on the closed physical half-space, and their initial value is the prescribed zero datum. Restricting the global solution gives the finite-time result.

A weak Euler solution on [0,T]\times\mathbb R^n consists of velocity u, pressure p, and a positive horizon T. For every smooth compactly supported vector field \varphi that vanishes at t=T, it satisfies

\int_0^T\!\int_{\mathbb R^n} \left[-u\cdot\partial_t\varphi -(u\otimes u):\nabla\varphi -p\,\nabla\cdot\varphi -f\cdot\varphi\right]dx\,dt =\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_0\cdot\varphi(0)\,dx.

At every t\in[0,T], the velocity slice is distributionally divergence-free, and the velocity, pressure, and forcing slices belong to spatial L^2. The prescribed initial velocity also belongs to L^2. The definition requires spatial integrability of the combined momentum integrand at every such time and time integrability of its spatial integral. The initial pairing is integrable by the L^2 datum and the compactly supported smooth test. It specifies the initial condition through the weak equation, without requiring u(0,\cdot)=u_0 for the chosen representative.

The definition is posed on a whole-space finite slab, allows general tests, keeps the pressure, and uses the initial-boundary and convection signs of Wiedemann's formulation.

For a smooth incompressible field, (u\cdot\nabla)u=\nabla\cdot(u\otimes u). Testing momentum and integrating by parts, when the integrations are justified, moves the derivatives onto \varphi; the initial term comes from the lower endpoint of the time integral. This explains both the minus signs and why the weak formulation can make sense without pointwise derivatives of u. Divergence-free tests also remove p\,\nabla\cdot\varphi, which gives the pressure-free formulation on the solenoidal space.

Proof for Theorem 8.29
uses 0

All four terms in the momentum integrand vanish pointwise, hence their space and time integrals are integrals of zero. The initial pairing is zero, every zero velocity slice belongs to L^2, and its distributional divergence is zero.

8.4.1.3. Pressure as an elliptic constraint🔗

Pressure has no separate evolution equation. Taking the divergence of Euler and using \nabla\cdot u=0 gives

-\Delta p =\nabla\mathbin\cdot\bigl((u\mathbin\cdot\nabla)u\bigr) -\nabla\mathbin\cdot f.

Thus pressure is determined nonlocally at each time, up to the boundary conditions and the usual additive constant. Hyperbolic transport and elliptic pressure recovery are already coupled before viscosity enters.

One way to read this constraint is to start with the acceleration a=f-(u\cdot\nabla)u. Momentum asks for \partial_tu=a-\nabla p, but an incompressible evolution must also have \nabla\cdot\partial_tu=0. Thus \Delta p=\nabla\cdot a: the pressure gradient corrects the acceleration so that it stays tangent to the divergence-free constraint. Solving that elliptic problem is the nonlocal step; knowing u at one point does not determine its pressure correction there.

On a bounded domain with homogeneous Dirichlet data, the weak Poisson theorem of the elliptic chapter gives a variational existence-and-uniqueness model for this elliptic step. Fluid pressure more often comes with periodic, whole-space, or Neumann data and an additive normalization, so that theorem supplies the analytic pattern rather than a direct pressure solver for every fluid domain.

The pressure Poisson source and residual are

S_p=\nabla_x\cdot((u\cdot\nabla_x)u)-\nabla_x\cdot f, \qquad R_p=-\Delta_xp-S_p.

The spatial subscript distinguishes these operators from derivatives in the time coordinate.

Proof for Theorem 8.31
uses 0

Taking spatial divergence gives \nabla_x\cdot\partial_tu+\nabla_x\cdot((u\cdot\nabla_x)u) +\Delta_xp=\nabla_x\cdot f. The first term vanishes for a sufficiently regular divergence-free flow. Rearranging the remaining scalar identity gives the stated Poisson equation.

8.4.1.4. Vorticity🔗

For a three-dimensional velocity field, set \omega=\nabla\times u. Taking the curl of the unforced Euler equation yields

\partial_t\omega+(u\cdot\nabla)\omega =(\omega\cdot\nabla)u.

The right-hand side stretches and tilts vortex lines. In two dimensions vorticity is scalar and this term disappears:

\partial_t\omega+u\cdot\nabla\omega=0.

This difference is one reason two-dimensional incompressible flow is more regular than its three-dimensional counterpart.

Proof for Theorem 8.33
uses 0

On the diagonal the two derivatives are identical and cancel. Exchanging i and j reverses the order of the same difference, hence changes its sign.

With vorticity scalar in the plane, the stretching term (\omega\cdot\nabla)u of the three-dimensional equation has no counterpart: the vorticity vector is normal to the plane of motion and the velocity does not vary in that direction. What remains is pure transport, and its residual is the material derivative of the scalar \omega.

R_\omega =\partial_t\omega+u\cdot\nabla\omega.

    Material-derivative residual ∂ₜω + u · ∇ω for the planar vorticity of a spacetime velocity field.

The residual is a definition; the content is that for solutions of the momentum equation it equals the curl of the force, hence vanishes in the unforced case. Taking the planar curl of \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\nabla p=f eliminates the pressure, because the curl of a gradient is zero, and incompressibility converts the curl of the convective term into transport of \omega. Since the derivation differentiates the momentum equation, it needs that equation on an open neighborhood rather than at a single point.

used by 1✓L∃∀N

Let u be jointly C^2 in space and time, let the pressure slice be C^2, and let the force slice be C^1. Suppose the momentum equation and \nabla\cdot u=0 hold on an open spatial neighborhood of x. For standard counterclockwise vorticity \omega=\partial_xu_2-\partial_yu_1,

\partial_t\omega+u\cdot\nabla\omega =\partial_x f_2-\partial_y f_1.

The clockwise-sign counterpart \omega_{\mathrm{cw}}=\partial_yu_1-\partial_xu_2=-\omega, used by the Boussinesq system, satisfies the same identity with the clockwise curl of the force on the right; the two statements differ by an overall sign, and the auxiliary commutation identities are proved in both conventions. In particular, either right-hand side vanishes for unforced planar Euler flow.

Proof for Theorem 8.35
uses 0

Differentiate the two momentum components in the transverse spatial directions and subtract. Joint C^2 regularity commutes the time and spatial derivatives. The pressure contribution vanishes because mixed derivatives commute. For a divergence-free planar velocity, the clockwise curl of (u\cdot\nabla)u is u\cdot\nabla\omega_{\mathrm{cw}}. What remains is exactly the clockwise curl of the force. Lean proves the clockwise form first; negating it gives the counterclockwise statement.

In three dimensions the curl of the convective term is not pure transport: the additional term (\omega\cdot\nabla)u survives and is responsible for vortex stretching. The general residual keeps that term and includes a viscous term, so Euler and Navier–Stokes flow share it.

For spacetime fields u,\omega:\mathbb R^{n+1}\to\mathbb R^n, with time in coordinate zero, the vortex-stretching term is the convective derivative of the velocity along \omega,

\bigl((\omega\cdot\nabla)u\bigr)_i=\sum_{j=1}^n\omega_j\,\partial_ju_i,

and the vorticity transport residual with viscosity \nu is the vector

R_\omega(\nu)=D_t^u\omega-(\omega\cdot\nabla)u-\nu\Delta_x\omega.

When n=3, \omega=\nabla\times u, and u is divergence free, R_\omega(0)=0 is the unforced Euler vorticity equation and R_\omega(\nu)=0 with \nu>0 is the Navier–Stokes vorticity equation. In the definition \omega is an independent vector field in any dimension; for Navier–Stokes flow its identification with the curl and with the two-form vorticity equation is a theorem.

The residual vanishes exactly when

Proof for Theorem 8.37
uses 0

Both statements are rearrangements in the additive group of vector fields: A-B-C=0 holds exactly when A=B+C, and the scalar multiple 0\cdot\Delta_x\omega vanishes.

8.4.1.5. Convective acceleration and Bernoulli's law🔗

At a point where every velocity component is differentiable, the gradient and antisymmetric parts of the velocity derivative separate convective acceleration into kinetic-energy and vorticity terms. With e=\frac12|u|^2 and \Omega_{ij}=\partial_ju_i-\partial_i u_j,

((u\cdot\nabla)u)_i =\partial_i e+\sum_j u_j\Omega_{ij}.

used by 1✓L∃∀N

Set B=p+e. At a point where the velocity components and pressure are differentiable, the steady, unforced balance (u\cdot\nabla)u+\nabla p=0 gives

u\cdot\nabla B=0.

Thus the Bernoulli function is constant along streamlines on which these hypotheses hold. If the flow is also irrotational at the point, then

((u\cdot\nabla)u)_i=\partial_i e.

The Euler balance then gives the stronger vector identity

\nabla\left(p+\frac12|u|^2\right)=0.

The theorem is pointwise; constancy of the Bernoulli function on a connected region follows when these derivatives vanish throughout that region.

Proof for Theorem 8.38
uses 0

Pair the steady momentum balance (u\cdot\nabla)u+\nabla p=0 with u. The convective-power identity gives u\cdot((u\cdot\nabla)u)=u\cdot\nabla e, hence u\cdot\nabla(e+p)=0.

For the irrotational strengthening, expand the vorticity contraction:

\partial_i e+\sum_j u_j(\partial_ju_i-\partial_i u_j).

The derivative of e is \sum_j u_j\partial_i u_j, so those terms cancel and leave \sum_j u_j\partial_j u_i. If the vorticity components vanish, the steady Euler component ((u\cdot\nabla)u)_i+\partial_i p=0 becomes \partial_i(e+p)=0.

8.4.1.6. Time-dependent potential flow🔗

The preceding calculation also works when an irrotational flow changes with time. Suppose we can write the velocity and force as spatial gradients, u=\nabla_xv and f=\nabla_xh. Mixed derivatives commute, so the time derivative of velocity is \nabla_xv_t; the convective acceleration is \nabla_x(|\nabla_xv|^2/2). The entire momentum equation is now one spatial gradient:

\nabla_x\!\left(v_t+\frac12|\nabla_xv|^2+p-h\right)=0.

We can make it vanish by choosing the pressure. Incompressibility leaves a separate condition on the potential: \Delta_xv=0. This is the potential-function reduction of Evans, §4.4.2.

In any spatial dimension, let v be C^2 at a spacetime point and let h be differentiable there. Define

u=\nabla_xv,\qquad p=h-v_t-\frac12|\nabla_xv|^2.

Then u is irrotational and satisfies the pointwise momentum equation

u_t+(u\cdot\nabla_x)u+\nabla_xp=\nabla_xh.

Moreover, \nabla_x\cdot u=0 exactly when \Delta_xv=0. On an open region with v\in C^2 and h\in C^1, the constructed velocity and pressure are C^1, so spatial harmonicity gives a classical Euler flow throughout that region.

Proof for Theorem 8.39
uses 1

The antisymmetric velocity derivative is zero because its two terms are mixed second derivatives of v. The irrotational convective-acceleration identity therefore turns (u\cdot\nabla_x)u into the kinetic-energy gradient. Commute time and space derivatives, then combine the four gradients in the momentum residual. Substituting the displayed pressure makes their scalar potential identically zero. Taking the divergence of \nabla_xv gives the spatial Laplacian directly.

Let v,h\in C^\infty(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n) and suppose \Delta_xv(t,x)=0 for t>0. Given Euler initial-value data with force \nabla_xh and initial velocity g(x)=\nabla_xv(0,x), the velocity u=\nabla_xv and pressure p=h-v_t-\frac12|\nabla_xv|^2 form a global smooth solution. In particular,

\lim_{\substack{(t,y)\to(0,x)\\t>0}}u(t,y)=g(x).

If spatial harmonicity is supplied at time zero as well, the data constructor derives distributional incompressibility of g from the classical divergence identity. The harmonic potential is part of the input.

Proof for Definition 8.40
uses 0

Differentiating a smooth potential preserves smoothness of the velocity; the time derivative and squared norm in the pressure do the same for pressure. The pointwise reduction supplies momentum balance and incompressibility at every positive time. Restriction of the smooth velocity to the initial slice gives the prescribed trace. At time zero, the classical-to-distributional divergence theorem turns the vanishing Laplacian into the initial data's weak incompressibility condition.

The time derivative in the pressure is visible in a simple planar example. Take v(t,x,y)=(1+t)(x^2-y^2) and zero force. Then

u=\bigl(2(1+t)x,-2(1+t)y\bigr),\qquad p=-(x^2-y^2)-2(1+t)^2(x^2+y^2).

The first pressure term balances u_t; the second balances convective acceleration. The compiled example PDE.Examples.Fluid.PotentialFlow checks the derivatives and harmonicity with the CAS, constructs the smooth solution, and checks its initial trace. Its velocity grows linearly in space, so the flow has infinite energy on the whole plane.

8.4.1.7. Exact solid rotation🔗

Consider the planar fields

u(x,y)=(-y,x),\qquad p(x,y)=\frac{x^2+y^2}{2}.

The velocity is divergence-free. Its convective acceleration is (u\cdot\nabla)u=(-x,-y), while \nabla p=(x,y), so pressure supplies the centripetal force. This flow is rotational rather than irrotational: \omega=2 and its Bernoulli function is p+\frac12|u|^2=x^2+y^2. It is constant along the circular streamlines, but not throughout the plane.

We reuse the polynomial differentiation from Foundations to check a vector equation and its pressure constraint. The pressure itself is not harmonic; its Laplacian balances the divergence of the convective acceleration. The same velocity has zero strain, which connects this flow to the symmetric-gradient energy example.

Proof for Theorem 8.41
uses 0

The divergence is \partial_x(-y)+\partial_yx=0. Direct differentiation gives

(u\cdot\nabla)u =(-y\partial_x+x\partial_y)(-y,x)=(-x,-y),

which cancels \nabla p=(x,y). The checked proof reflects these polynomial expressions, differentiates them symbolically, and closes the normalized identities with cas. It also verifies -\Delta p=-2 and \nabla\cdot((u\cdot\nabla)u)=-2.

The exact momentum proof is a one-line tactic call:

-- Prove the exact vector momentum residual is zero. open CAS.Certificate open NavierStokes.Symbolic example : ResidualBound solidRotationEulerMomentumResidual2.vectorFn Set.univ 0 := ⊢ ResidualBound solidRotationEulerMomentumResidual2.vectorFn Set.univ 0 All goals completed! 🐙

The four spatial derivatives are 0,-1,1,0. In each strain component the off-diagonal derivatives cancel and the diagonal derivative is zero. The certified energy expression is therefore a sum of zero squares.

8.4.2. Inviscid Boussinesq Flow🔗

The inviscid Boussinesq system couples incompressible momentum to an advected scalar. In the vertical-buoyancy convention used here,

\partial_t u+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\nabla p=\theta e_2, \qquad \nabla\cdot u=0, \qquad \partial_t\theta+u\cdot\nabla\theta=0.

Chen and Hou introduce the upper-half-plane vorticity–streamfunction system and its dynamic rescaling in §2.1, equations (2.3)–(2.7) Chen and Hou (2022). We keep that formulation separate from the standard primitive velocity–pressure equations: the buoyancy orientation and scalar-vorticity sign are explicit. A checked curl calculation identifies exactly which primitive convention yields the paper's vorticity source. The dynamic rescaling of the upper-half-plane equations, its normalization, and an independent fixed-power primitive calculation are checked as well, and the half-plane Green potential inverts the Poisson problem for compactly supported C^2 sources with an odd extension across the boundary.

The scalar drives rotation through its horizontal variation. With the counterclockwise convention \omega=\partial_1u_2-\partial_2u_1, taking curl of the displayed buoyancy force gives \partial_1\theta. A spatially constant temperature has zero curl and its force can be absorbed into the pressure by replacing p with p-\theta x_2. For sufficiently smooth fields, differentiating the transport equation gives

(\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla)\nabla\theta =-(\nabla u)^{\mathsf T}\nabla\theta.

Temperature is constant along each particle path, yet its gradient can grow as neighboring paths stretch and compress. That growing gradient feeds the vorticity equation, whose velocity in turn transports the temperature. The feedback explains why the transported scalar remains dynamically active. Reversing the curl or buoyancy convention reverses the corresponding source sign.

For the rescaling calculation, it is useful to eliminate pressure and recover velocity from a streamfunction. With C^2 regularity, its mixed partials cancel in the divergence, while taking curl leaves a Laplacian with a sign determined by our convention. Recovering the streamfunction from vorticity then requires solving a Poisson problem in the half-plane.

Proof for Theorem 8.46
uses 0

Expand the two velocity components. The divergence is -\partial_1\partial_2\phi+\partial_2\partial_1\phi, which vanishes by the C^2 mixed-partial theorem. Expanding either scalar curl leaves the two diagonal second derivatives with the corresponding sign.

With the sign fixed, the paper's system can be stated in the three scalar unknowns (\omega,\theta,\phi): the clockwise vorticity is transported and driven by \partial_1\theta, the temperature is transported, and the streamfunction is tied to \omega by a Dirichlet problem on the upper half-plane. Velocity appears only as (-\partial_2\phi,\partial_1\phi).

On \mathbb R^2_+=\{x_2>0\}, the physical equations are

\partial_t\omega+u\cdot\nabla\omega=\partial_1\theta, \qquad \partial_t\theta+u\cdot\nabla\theta=0, \qquad -\Delta\phi=\omega.

The boundary trace is \phi(x_1,0,t)=0. The fields are defined on the whole plane. Vorticity and temperature are jointly C^1 on the admitted times, with ambient time differentiability there; every streamfunction slice is spatially C^2. No joint time regularity of the streamfunction is required. The equations are imposed only in the open upper half-plane.

Proof for Theorem 8.48
uses 0

The first two claims are the planar streamfunction identities. For the boundary claim, restrict \phi to the horizontal coordinate line. Its trace is the constant zero function, so its tangential derivative \partial_1\phi vanishes. This derivative is precisely the normal velocity component.

The primitive and vorticity-stream formulations are related by taking the clockwise curl of the momentum equation. The pressure drops out, incompressibility turns the curl of the convective term into u\cdot\nabla\omega, and the buoyancy \kappa\theta e_2 contributes -\kappa\,\partial_1\theta; matching this with the paper's source +\partial_1\theta is what pins down the buoyancy orientation.

Assume u is jointly C^2 on spacetime and, at the time considered, p and \theta are respectively C^2 and C^1 on the whole plane. If the primitive momentum force is \kappa\theta e_2 and clockwise vorticity is \omega=\partial_2u_1-\partial_1u_2, then on every open spatial domain where the primitive momentum equation and incompressibility hold,

\partial_t\omega+u\cdot\nabla\omega=-\kappa\,\partial_1\theta.

Thus the paper's positive source is the downward-buoyancy choice \kappa=-1. Under that convention, with a supplied C^2 streamfunction satisfying u=(-\partial_2\phi,\partial_1\phi) and the zero boundary trace, a primitive solution with jointly continuously differentiable temperature solving both the momentum equation with force -\theta e_2 and the temperature transport equation induces the full upper-half-plane vorticity–streamfunction solution predicate.

Proof for Theorem 8.49
uses 0

Take clockwise curl locally inside the open spatial domain. Equality on a neighborhood gives equality of the required coordinate derivatives, while mixed derivatives cancel the pressure curl. For a divergence-free planar velocity, the curl of the convective term is u\cdot\nabla\omega; the vertical force contributes -\kappa\partial_1\theta. The streamfunction identities then provide incompressibility and -\Delta\phi=\omega, while the primitive scalar transport equation and zero trace give the remaining solution fields and boundary condition.

Self-similar blow-up is studied by rescaling space, time, and the amplitudes of \omega and \theta with time-dependent factors, with the aim that a solution collapsing to the origin becomes one converging to a stationary profile. The factors are not free: the streamfunction scale is forced by -\Delta\phi=\omega, and transforming the source \partial_1\theta requires the amplitude relation C_\theta C_l=C_\omega^2.

The sign of the length rate determines whether these coordinates shrink or expand in physical space. The De Gregorio blowup in the companion repository BlowupZoo gives an expanding real-line example with the corresponding physical clock.

At rescaled time \tau, set

\widetilde\omega(x,\tau)=C_\omega\omega(C_lx,t(\tau)),\qquad \widetilde\theta(x,\tau)=C_\theta\theta(C_lx,t(\tau)),

\widetilde\phi(x,\tau)=C_\omega C_l^{-2}\phi(C_lx,t(\tau)).

The scale laws are C_\omega'=c_\omega C_\omega, C_l'=-c_lC_l, C_\theta'=c_\theta C_\theta, and t'=C_\omega, together with C_\theta C_l=C_\omega^2 and c_\theta=c_l+2c_\omega, with C_l>0 so dilation preserves the upper half-plane. The complete transformed-system predicate reuses the canonical pair of rescaled scalar equations and adds the streamfunction Poisson equation and zero boundary trace.

✓L∃∀N

For rate functions c_l,c_\omega,c_\theta, the rescaled transport velocity is

V(x,\tau)=c_l(\tau)x+u(x,\tau).

The scalar part of the rescaled system is the pair of pointwise equations

\partial_\tau\omega+V\cdot\nabla\omega =c_\omega\omega+\partial_1\theta, \qquad \partial_\tau\theta+V\cdot\nabla\theta=c_\theta\theta.

The equations are stated for arbitrary rate functions, independently of any particular scaling data, and may be imposed either at one time or on a specified space-time domain. The two residual functions are the left side minus the right side of the corresponding equation.

Each rescaled scalar equation holds on a domain exactly when its pointwise residual vanishes throughout that domain.

L_\omega=R_\omega\text{ on }\Omega \Longleftrightarrow \mathcal R_\omega=0\text{ on }\Omega, \qquad L_\theta=R_\theta\text{ on }\Omega \Longleftrightarrow \mathcal R_\theta=0\text{ on }\Omega.

Proof for Theorem 8.52
uses 0

Expand the residual as the left side minus the right side and rearrange.

The equations are imposed only in the open half-plane, yet the normalization reads off derivatives at the origin, which lies on the boundary. For fields smooth across the boundary the gap is closed by continuity: an identity between continuous functions that holds on a set persists on its closure, and the same argument applies to its spatial derivatives.

uses 1used by 1✓L∃∀N

For globally continuously differentiable representatives, either rescaled scalar equation holding on a spatial domain also holds on its closure. If the domain is open, then with one further degree of regularity for each spatial differentiation, the once-differentiated vorticity equation and twice-differentiated temperature equation extend to the closure as well. This applies in particular to the open upper half-plane.

Writing L_\omega=\partial_\tau\omega+V\cdot\nabla\omega, R_\omega=c_\omega\omega+\partial_1\theta, L_\theta=\partial_\tau\theta+V\cdot\nabla\theta, and R_\theta=c_\theta\theta, the conclusions are

L_\omega=R_\omega\text{ on }\Omega \Longrightarrow L_\omega=R_\omega\text{ and }\partial_iL_\omega=\partial_iR_\omega \text{ on }\overline{\Omega},

L_\theta=R_\theta\text{ on }\Omega \Longrightarrow L_\theta=R_\theta\text{ and } \partial_i\partial_jL_\theta=\partial_i\partial_jR_\theta \text{ on }\overline{\Omega}.

Proof for Theorem 8.53
uses 0

Both sides of each interior identity are continuous. Equality therefore passes to the closure. On an open domain, the differentiated statements follow by first differentiating the equality and then applying the same closure argument to the continuous derivative fields.

The rescaled equations become a theorem rather than a definition once the scale laws are imposed. Differentiating the pullbacks by the chain rule, the dilation term comes from C_l'=-c_lC_l, the amplitude terms from C_\omega' and C_\theta', and the physical time derivative enters through t'=C_\omega; the amplitude compatibility is what makes the transformed source match the transformed advection terms.

A classical upper-half-plane solution on an open physical-time set satisfies the following transformed system at every rescaled time whose physical-time image belongs to that set and at which the scale laws hold:

\partial_\tau\widetilde\omega+ (c_lx+\widetilde u)\cdot\nabla\widetilde\omega =c_\omega\widetilde\omega+\partial_1\widetilde\theta,

\partial_\tau\widetilde\theta+ (c_lx+\widetilde u)\cdot\nabla\widetilde\theta =c_\theta\widetilde\theta, \qquad -\Delta\widetilde\phi=\widetilde\omega,

with the zero streamfunction boundary trace preserved.

    A classical solution on an open physical time set gives a solution of the dynamically rescaled system at times mapping into that set and satisfying the scale laws.

    The conclusion includes the vorticity and temperature equations on the open half-plane and the streamfunction equation and its zero boundary condition. The physical time set is assumed open so that the joint C¹ hypotheses provide ordinary, rather than merely relative, derivatives. This is the forward change-of-variables implication.

Proof for Theorem 8.54
uses 0

Differentiate the three pullbacks. The derivative of C_lx contributes -c_l C_lx, which cancels advection by c_lx. The reconstructed velocity has scale C_\omega C_l^{-1}. Vorticity advection and the physical vorticity time-derivative term both carry C_\omega^2; temperature advection carries C_\omega C_\theta. The source derivative carries C_\theta C_l, equal to C_\omega^2 by compatibility. The streamfunction scale contributes C_\omega C_l^{-2}C_l^2=C_\omega, preserving the Poisson equation. Positive C_l preserves the upper half-plane, and the boundary trace remains zero under tangential dilation.

The normalization also relies on symmetry: the paper's profile has odd vorticity and even temperature under reflection in the vertical axis. Vorticity parity does not automatically pass to the streamfunction, because \phi is determined by \omega only through the Dirichlet problem. The reflected and negated streamfunction solves the same problem, so uniqueness in a suitable class transfers the parity.

Let R(x_1,x_2)=(-x_1,x_2) and let \mathcal A be an admissible class of whole-plane streamfunctions, closed under \phi\mapsto-\phi\circ R. Suppose \phi\in\mathcal A is C^2 on the whole plane and the Dirichlet problem is unique in \mathcal A. Then

-\Delta\phi=\omega\text{ in }\mathbb H,\qquad \phi|_{\partial\mathbb H}=0,\qquad \omega\circ R=-\omega \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \phi\circ R=-\phi.

The theorem keeps \mathcal A explicit. Uniqueness among all smooth functions on the unbounded half-plane would be false without a decay, energy, or representation condition.

Proof for Theorem 8.55
uses 0

The Laplacian is invariant under R, so -\phi\circ R solves the same Poisson equation as \phi. It has the same zero boundary trace and remains in \mathcal A by reflection stability. Uniqueness in \mathcal A gives -\phi\circ R=\phi.

Uniqueness is an assumption in the previous theorem. When the streamfunction is given explicitly by the half-plane Green function, the same parity can instead be read off from the kernel: reflection preserves the half-plane and the method-of-images kernel, so oddness of the source transfers to the potential directly.

used by 1✓L∃∀N

If \omega is odd under R(x_1,x_2)=(-x_1,x_2) and its method-of-images Green integrand is integrable at every field point, then

\phi(x)=\int_{\mathbb H}G_{\mathbb H}(y,x)\omega(y)\,dy

is odd under R and has zero horizontal boundary trace. These conclusions are proved from kernel geometry. Normal oddness together with integrability of \Phi_2(x-\cdot)\omega identifies the same integral with the whole-space convolution, without compact support. If, in addition, \omega is a compactly supported C^2 whole-space function, then the integral is C^2 and satisfies -\Delta\phi=\omega on the upper half-plane. The approximate profile of the paper has a nonintegrable r^{\bar\alpha_1}\simeq r^{-1/3} far field, which Section 7.2.1 treats by a semi-analytic homogeneous streamfunction and an angular Dirichlet ODE before estimating a faster-decaying numerical remainder.

Proof for Theorem 8.56
uses 0

Apply the generic half-space potential theorem to reflection in coordinate zero. This reflection preserves x_2>0; kernel invariance and the measure-preserving change of variables transfer oddness of \omega to \phi. Boundary cancellation is pointwise in the source variable before integration. Under the normal odd-extension hypothesis, the planar method-of-images theorem identifies the potential with \Phi_2*\omega whenever that convolution is integrable. The compact C^2 inversion theorem then proves the pointwise Poisson equation.

The semi-analytic far-field ansatz in Section 7.2.1 is governed by the exact polar identity

-\Delta_{\mathrm{pol}}\bigl(r^{2+\bar\alpha_1}f(\beta)\bigr) =r^{\bar\alpha_1} \left(-f''(\beta)-(2+\bar\alpha_1)^2f(\beta)\right).

Thus the angular Dirichlet equation (-\partial_\beta^2-(2+\bar\alpha_1)^2)f=g_1 produces the uncut source r^{\bar\alpha_1}g_1(\beta) at positive radii. Lean proves this homogeneous polar calculation. It also proves the exact commutator introduced by the radial cutoff \chi: the extra terms involve only \Delta_{\mathrm{rad}}\chi and \chi'. A general C^2 pullback theorem identifies this polar operator with the Cartesian Euclidean Laplacian away from r=0. These identities are the homogeneous polar Laplacian theorem.

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

Let g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R be continuous, set L=\pi/2, and suppose -2<\alpha<0. With a=2+\alpha, there is a classical solution

-f''-a^2f=g,\qquad f(0)=f(L)=0.

The construction keeps the resonance condition explicit. Define

\begin{aligned} C(\beta)&=\int_0^\beta\cos(as)g(s)\,ds,\\ S(\beta)&=\int_0^\beta\sin(as)g(s)\,ds. \end{aligned}

Then

\begin{aligned} f(\beta)&=A\sin(a\beta)\\ &\quad+\frac{\cos(a\beta)S(\beta)-\sin(a\beta)C(\beta)}{a},\\ A&=\frac{\sin(aL)C(L)-\cos(aL)S(L)}{a\sin(aL)}. \end{aligned}

Here 0<a<2, so 0<aL<\pi and the denominator is nonzero. Continuous forcing gives f\in C^2. If |g|\leq M on [0,L], with M\geq0, the formula also gives the explicit sufficient bound for 0\leq\beta\leq L:

|f(\beta)|\leq\frac{2ML}{a} \left(1+\frac1{|\sin(aL)|}\right).

On the same interval, its first derivative satisfies

|f'(\beta)|\leq2ML\left(1+\frac1{|\sin(aL)|}\right).

The homogeneous streamfunction r^{2+\alpha}f(\beta) therefore has negative polar Laplacian r^\alpha g(\beta) for r>0. A certified residual gives a quantitative correction as well. Let q\in C^2 have exact zero endpoint values and suppose

|g+q''+a^2q|\leq\delta\quad\text{on }[0,L].

Apply the same inverse to this residual and add the correction to q. The result satisfies the exact forced equation and boundary values, with value error at most 2\delta L(1+1/|\sin(aL)|)/a and first-derivative error at most 2\delta L(1+1/|\sin(aL)|). Thus a tighter residual certificate improves both error bounds through the same theorem.

The inverse also gives a Cartesian field. For positive radius and -\pi<\beta<\pi, the inverse polar Jacobian proves C^2 regularity of the reconstructed streamfunction. The local chart round trip then gives

-\Delta U(r\cos\beta,r\sin\beta)=r^\alpha g(\beta).

This excludes the origin and the chart's negative horizontal cut. If the forcing is odd about L, then the solution is odd there too: f(2L-\beta)=-f(\beta) and f''(L)=0. Uniqueness follows from the conserved energy of the difference of two oscillator solutions with the same initial value and slope. These are tangential angular identities; the normal extension of the source vorticity can jump at the physical boundary and needs a separate weak argument.

Proof for Theorem 8.57
uses 0

Differentiate the two integrals by the fundamental theorem of calculus. The terms involving g cancel in the first derivative and combine to -g in the second, giving the forced equation. At the left endpoint both integrals vanish; the chosen amplitude cancels the value at the right endpoint. Bounding sine and cosine by one bounds each integral by M\beta and gives the displayed estimate. The homogeneous polar identity then supplies the radial factor.

Let R(x_1,x_2)=(-x_1,x_2) and u=(-\partial_2\phi,\partial_1\phi). If a C^1 streamfunction is odd under R, then

\partial_2\phi(Rx)=-\partial_2\phi(x),\qquad \partial_1\phi(Rx)=\partial_1\phi(x),

and therefore u_1(Rx)=-u_1(x) while u_2(Rx)=u_2(x). If in addition \phi(x_1,0)=0, then u_2(x_1,0)=0. Thus the scalar symmetries together with odd streamfunction parity and the Dirichlet trace imply all velocity conditions used by the normalization calculation.

Proof for Theorem 8.58
uses 0

Differentiate \phi\circ R=-\phi. Tangential differentiation introduces one sign from R and one from oddness, while normal differentiation introduces only the sign from oddness. The boundary identity follows by differentiating the zero trace tangentially.

Dynamic rescaling leaves the rates c_l,c_\omega,c_\theta undetermined. The paper fixes two of them by requiring the origin traces \omega_x(0) and \theta_{xx}(0) to stay constant in time, the third being the compatibility law c_\theta=c_l+2c_\omega, and the symmetry bridge supplies the velocity conditions this calculation uses. Because division is totalized in Lean, the nondegeneracy \omega_x(0)\ne0 that makes the quotient meaningful is carried as an explicit hypothesis.

At the origin write \omega_x=\partial_1\omega, \theta_{xx}=\partial_1^2\theta, and u_x=\partial_1u_1. The normalization is

c_l=\frac{2\theta_{xx}(0)}{\omega_x(0)},\qquad c_\omega=\frac12c_l+u_x(0),\qquad c_\theta=c_l+2c_\omega,

with the necessary condition \omega_x(0)\ne0. The accompanying symmetry predicates distinguish the minimal cancellations used at the origin from the streamfunction-level assumptions that imply them.

    structure Boussinesq.SatisfiesRescalingNormalizationAt
  (fields : Boussinesq.VorticityStreamFields)
  (spatialRate vorticityRate temperatureRate : ℝ → ℝ) (t : ℝ) : Prop
    structure Boussinesq.SatisfiesRescalingNormalizationAt
  (fields :
    Boussinesq.VorticityStreamFields)
  (spatialRate vorticityRate
    temperatureRate : ℝ → ℝ)
  (t : ℝ) : Prop

    The three normalization identities of the dynamic rescaling at one time: the dilation rate is 2 θ_xx(0)/ω_x(0), the vorticity amplitude rate is half of it plus u_x(0), and the temperature amplitude rate is the dilation rate plus twice the vorticity rate. These are the conditions (2.9) of Chen and Hou.

    Fields

    vorticity_x_at_origin_ne_zero : Boussinesq.vorticityXAtOrigin fields t ≠ 0

    The vorticity trace used as the denominator is nonzero.

    spatial_rate_eq : spatialRate t = 2 * Boussinesq.temperatureXXAtOrigin fields t / Boussinesq.vorticityXAtOrigin fields t

    The spatial dilation rate is fixed by the two origin traces.

    vorticity_rate_eq : vorticityRate t = spatialRate t / 2 + Boussinesq.tangentialVelocityXAtOrigin fields t

    The vorticity amplitude rate is fixed by dilation and velocity strain.

    temperature_rate_eq : temperatureRate t = spatialRate t + 2 * vorticityRate t

    The temperature amplitude rate satisfies the scaling compatibility law.

Whether the traces are in fact preserved is decided by their evolution equations. Differentiating the rescaled vorticity equation once and the temperature equation twice in x_1 and evaluating at the origin, the symmetry conditions remove the normal and undifferentiated transport terms and leave two linear scalar ODEs in which the rates appear as coefficients.

For sufficiently smooth space-time fields satisfying the rescaled equations on the open upper half-plane and the stated symmetries,

\frac{d}{d\tau}\omega_x(0)= (c_\omega-c_l-u_x(0))\omega_x(0)+\theta_{xx}(0),

\frac{d}{d\tau}\theta_{xx}(0)= \bigl(c_\theta-2(c_l+u_x(0))\bigr)\theta_{xx}(0).

These are derived from equation (2.8) by differentiating in the tangential direction, extending the differentiated identities continuously to the origin, and commuting space and time derivatives. The fields are represented by smooth extensions across the boundary, but the equations are assumed only on the open upper half-plane.

Proof for Theorem 8.60
uses 0

Differentiate the vorticity equation once and the temperature equation twice in the tangential variable. At the origin, parity and the two zero traces remove the normal and undifferentiated transport terms. Expanding the remaining advection products gives the two displayed scalar ODEs.

Substitution of the three normalization identities makes both trace-ODE right-hand sides zero. Hence, on an open connected time domain where the regularity, upper-half-plane equations, symmetries, and normalization hold at every time,

Proof for Theorem 8.61
uses 0

The first normalization identity implies c_l\omega_x(0)=2\theta_{xx}(0). Together with the formulas for c_\omega and c_\theta, elementary algebra cancels both ODE right-hand sides. A differentiable real-valued function whose derivative vanishes on an open connected set is constant there.

Constant rates make the rescaled equations autonomous; a stationary profile is an additional condition. The fixed-power construction starts with time-independent primitive profiles and a single exponent \lambda. The exponents of \theta and p are forced by requiring buoyancy and pressure to balance \partial_tu. This ansatz is checked against the primitive classical predicate rather than the vorticity-stream model.

uses 1used by 1✓L∃∀N

For an exponent \lambda and profiles U,\Theta,P, set

y=\frac{x}{(1-t)^{1+\lambda}},\qquad u=(1-t)^\lambda U(y),\qquad \theta=(1-t)^{\lambda-1}\Theta(y),\qquad p=(1-t)^{2\lambda}P(y).

The ansatz is an instance of the common backward-similarity transformation. The quotient formula is used analytically only for t<1, where the real-power base is positive.

  (profile :
    Boussinesq.SelfSimilarProfile) :

    Convert similarity profiles into physical-space Boussinesq fields.

Substituting the ansatz into the Boussinesq system, every term of the momentum equation carries the factor (1-t)^{\lambda-1}, every term of the temperature equation carries (1-t)^{\lambda-2}, and time differentiation of the profiles produces the scaling terms -\lambda U+(1+\lambda)(y\cdot\nabla)U and (1-\lambda)\Theta+(1+\lambda)y\cdot\nabla\Theta. Dividing out the powers leaves a stationary system in the similarity variable.

The stationary profile equations are

\nabla\cdot U=0,

-\lambda U+(1+\lambda)(y\cdot\nabla)U +(U\cdot\nabla)U+\nabla P-\Theta e_2=0,

(1-\lambda)\Theta+(1+\lambda)y\cdot\nabla\Theta +U\cdot\nabla\Theta=0.

The profile predicate also requires global first-order classical regularity; the residual equalities alone would otherwise use totalized derivatives.

    def Boussinesq.IsClassicalSelfSimilarProfile
  (profile :
    Boussinesq.SelfSimilarProfile) :
  Prop

    A classical self-similar profile is first-order regular and solves all reduced equations.

The reduction is exact rather than asymptotic: each physical residual is a nonzero power of 1-t times the corresponding profile residual, so for t<1 vanishing of one is equivalent to vanishing of the other. The direction checked here goes from profile to physical solution, including the transfer of regularity.

Proof for Theorem 8.64
uses 0

Differentiate the backward ansatz using the common similarity chain rule. Velocity time differentiation, convection, pressure gradient, and buoyancy all carry the factor (1-t)^{\lambda-1}. Temperature time differentiation and temperature advection both carry (1-t)^{\lambda-2}, while divergence carries (1-t)^{-1}. The three physical residuals are therefore these nonzero factors times the three reduced residuals. The regularity part follows by composing the C^1 profiles with the smooth positive backward power scales on t<1.

8.4.2.1. Approximate responses with exact error accounting🔗

The stability argument in Chen–Hou separates a leading evolution from a finite-rank perturbation. The response to each perturbation column is a spatial field evolving in time. Section 2.8 explains how to use a computed response while preserving the exact evolution equation Chen and Hou (2022).

Write L for the full linearized operator, \chi for the prescribed response columns, G(t) for their approximation, and a(t) for their coefficients. The response contribution is

\widehat W_2(t)=\int_0^t G(t-s)a(s)\,ds.

Its error includes both the initial mismatch and the evolution residual:

R(t)=(G(0)-\chi)a(t) +\int_0^t \bigl(G'(t-s)-LG(t-s)\bigr)a(s)\,ds.

uses 0used by 0✓L∃∀N

For a continuously differentiable response and continuous coefficients, \widehat W_2'=L\widehat W_2+\chi a+R. If the complementary trajectory satisfies W_1'=LW_1-\chi a-R, their sum solves W'=LW exactly and has the initial value of W_1.

The general statement evaluates values and spatial evolution through bounded maps from a regularity space into the equation space. It does not assume that L is bounded on the equation space. A bound \eta on the initial mismatch and a time-dependent bound \varepsilon on the response residual give

\|R(t)\|\leq\eta\|a(t)\| +\int_0^t\|a(s)\|\varepsilon(t-s)\,ds,\qquad t\geq0.

Proof for Theorem 8.66
uses 0

The moving-endpoint integral rule gives the initial-response term and the integral of the response derivative. Subtract the spatial evolution inside the integral and retain the difference in R. Adding the complementary equation cancels the forcing and error. The norm estimate follows from the operator bounds and the Bochner integral inequality.

8.4.2.2. Analytic correction before weighted estimates🔗

Small numerical errors can change a function's vanishing order. For example, f(x)=\delta x+x^3 has a small linear coefficient, but |f(x)|/|x|^3 is unbounded near zero whenever \delta\neq0. A singular weight therefore needs exact cancellation of the low-order terms before numerical bounds are applied.

Let Q extract the derivative traces that must vanish, and let \Psi reconstruct correction fields with Q\Psi=\mathrm{id}. For an approximate trajectory g, set M=QL\Psi and solve the coefficient equation

a'=Ma-Q(g'-Lg),\qquad a(0)=-Q(g(0)-\chi).

✓L∃∀N

For a field in the bounded C^{k,\gamma} space on \Omega, evaluation of all derivatives through order k at a point x\in\overline\Omega is a bounded linear map into the finite coefficient space with its maximum norm:

Q_x f=(D^\alpha f(x))_{|\alpha|\leq k},\qquad \|Q_x\|\leq1.

The bound uses the Hölder graph norm. At a boundary point, the derivative values are the continuous extensions of the interior derivatives. Selecting the required coordinates gives a trace map for the correction; constructing its right inverse still requires the chosen spatial correction fields. If \Omega is open and convex, the fields of order below k have the prescribed derivatives within \overline\Omega. This also identifies the traces with boundary derivatives, without extending the function across the boundary. For a field with two further derivatives available, differentiating its assembled gradient within the closure gives its assembled Hessian.

Ordinary formulas v_\alpha can define a field in this space directly. On an open \Omega, require continuity on the closure, the successor derivative identities in the interior, uniform bounds \|v_\alpha\|_\infty\leq C_\alpha, and top-order Hölder bounds [v_\alpha]_\gamma\leq H_\alpha. The construction preserves the given interior derivatives and boundary traces. Its graph norm is at most B when every C_\alpha\leq B and every top-order C_\alpha+H_\alpha\leq B. Evans's derivative-sum norm satisfies

\begin{aligned} \|f\|_{\mathrm{Evans}}&\leq\sum_{|\alpha|\leq k}C_\alpha\\ &\quad+\sum_{|\alpha|=k}H_\alpha. \end{aligned}

For a top-order field with Lipschitz constant L_\alpha, interpolation supplies the bound

H_\alpha=(2C_\alpha)^{1-\gamma}L_\alpha^\gamma.

The value and Lipschitz bounds are uniform on the closure; the domain may be unbounded. These per-field constants are inputs, so improving their certificates does not change the construction or the norm comparison.

Proof for Theorem 8.67
uses 0

Project each derivative field and evaluate its continuous extension at x. Each value is bounded by the corresponding uniform norm, which is bounded by the graph norm. Taking the maximum preserves that bound. For the boundary derivative, use the interior derivative relation and the continuity of its assembled gradient on the closure. The mean value estimate on a convex domain extends differentiability to the boundary with that limiting gradient. Differentiate the finite coordinate sum to obtain the Hessian relation. For the construction, bundle the bounded continuous fields and their top-order Hölder representatives. Each zero extension agrees locally with its ordinary formula at interior points, so the supplied derivative identities give graph compatibility. Taking maxima or summing the supplied budgets gives the two norm bounds. Interpolate the range bound 2C_\alpha at exponent zero with the Lipschitz bound at exponent one to obtain the stated Hölder constant.

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

A proposed spatial reconstruction \Phi can first be made exact. Suppose its coordinate residual satisfies

\|\mathrm{id}-Q\Phi\|\leq\delta<1.

The Neumann inverse defines \Psi=\Phi(Q\Phi)^{-1} and gives Q\Psi=\mathrm{id}. The correction retains quantitative bounds:

\begin{aligned} \|\Psi\|&\leq\frac{\|\Phi\|}{1-\delta},\\ \|\Psi-\Phi\|&\leq\frac{\|\Phi\|\delta}{1-\delta},\\ \|L\Psi\|&\leq\frac{\|L\Phi\|}{1-\delta}. \end{aligned}

Only the coefficient space must be complete. A finite-dimensional application therefore needs a certified residual bound, rather than an exact inverse matrix. The residual must use the coefficient space's operator norm; for the full derivative trace map above, the coefficient norm is the maximum norm.

On a closed time interval [0,T], suppose the approximate trajectory is differentiable within the interval and its extracted residual is continuous. With this exact reconstruction, the coefficient equation has an exact solution. The corrected trajectory \widetilde g=g+\Psi a has zero extracted initial error, and

\begin{aligned} \widetilde g'&=L\widetilde g+\widetilde R,\\ \widetilde R&=(\mathrm{id}-\Psi Q)(g'-L\widetilde g),\\ Q\widetilde R&=0. \end{aligned}

The general version includes the value map between the two regularity spaces. It allows any complete normed coefficient space. The spatial correction fields need not be eigenfunctions: their remaining evolution error stays in \widetilde R. Only data on [0,T] are required; at its endpoints the evolution equation uses the corresponding one-sided time derivative.

The same exact coefficient solution has quantitative bounds. Let U(t,s) be the propagator of a'=Ma. For a fixed 0\leq t\leq T, suppose

\begin{aligned} \|U(t,s)\|&\leq C_t(s),\\ \|Q(g'(s)-Lg(s))\|&\leq\varepsilon(s),\\ 0&\leq s\leq t, \end{aligned}

and C_t\varepsilon is integrable. Then

\begin{aligned} \|a(t)\|&\leq C_t(0)\|Q(g(0)-\chi)\|\\ &\quad+\int_0^t C_t(s)\varepsilon(s)\,ds. \end{aligned}

Keeping the envelopes inside the integral preserves their time dependence. The remaining spatial error obeys

\begin{aligned} \|\widetilde R(t)\|&\leq\|\mathrm{id}-\Psi Q\|\\ &\quad\cdot\bigl(\|g'(t)-Lg(t)\|\\ &\qquad+\|L\Psi\|\|a(t)\|\bigr). \end{aligned}

These estimates keep the correction's contribution explicit. Sharper bounds on the propagator, extracted residual, or spatial correction can be supplied to the same analytic theorem.

          Q
              (PDE.Analysis.Evolution.responseJetResidual
                J A Q Ψ g g' a t) =

Proof for Theorem 8.68
uses 0

The coordinate residual has norm below one, so its geometric series converges and inverts Q\Phi. Composing with \Phi gives the exact right inverse. The geometric-series norm bound gives the reconstruction estimates; applying L before taking the norm retains the sharper bound on L\Phi. Use variation of constants for the bounded coefficient operator M, integrating only over the prescribed time interval. The fundamental theorem of calculus within a closed interval gives the derivative at its endpoints as well. Differentiate g+\Psi a, substitute the coefficient equation, and apply Q\Psi=\mathrm{id}. This cancels the extracted traces while leaving the full residual explicit. Apply the propagator formula and the integral norm inequality to bound the coefficients. Apply the projection bound to the full corrected residual to bound its remaining spatial error.

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

Suppose a field's value, gradient, and Hessian vanish at the origin, it is C^3 near every point of the segment from 0 to x, and its third derivative has operator norm at most K along that segment. Then, for x\neq0,

\frac{\|f(x)\|}{\|x\|^3}\leq\frac K6.

A more general variant uses supplied derivative fields D and H within the segment. If f(0)=D(0)=0 and

\|H(y)\|\leq K\|y\|,\qquad y\in[0,x],

the same cubic bound holds. Here D is the derivative of f and H is the derivative of D within the segment. This allows a segment that starts on or lies along the domain boundary; no smooth extension across that boundary is needed. The Hessian envelope can be verified directly, without differentiating H.

These estimates apply to vector-valued fields on any real normed space and retain the factor 1/6 for numerical error budgets.

For a scalar field in the bounded C^{k,\gamma} space on an open convex domain, apply the estimate to D^\alpha f whenever |\alpha|+2\leq k. Its gradient and Hessian are already supplied by the derivative graph, even at the boundary. The Hessian's coordinate matrix satisfies

\begin{aligned} A_\alpha(y)_{ij}&=D^{\alpha+e_i+e_j}f(y),\\ \|H_\alpha(y)\|&=\|A_\alpha(y)\|_{2\to2}. \end{aligned}

Thus a certified Euclidean matrix norm bound supplies the required Hessian envelope with its original constant. This is the Euclidean operator norm, rather than an entrywise or row-sum norm. The value and first-derivative traces of D^\alpha f must vanish exactly at the base point. Tighter numerical envelopes can be supplied to the same analytic theorem.

Proof for Theorem 8.69
uses 0

Parametrize the segment by \gamma(t)=tx, 0\leq t\leq1. Compare the operator-valued derivative with the quadratic majorant to obtain \|D(tx)\|\leq K\|x\|^2t^2/2. A second mean value comparison gives \|f(tx)\|\leq K\|x\|^3t^3/6. Both comparisons use derivatives within the segment, including its endpoints. For the smooth version, the third derivative bound and the zero Hessian at the origin supply the required Hessian envelope. Set t=1 and divide by the positive factor \|x\|^3. For the Hölder fields, assemble the derivatives by finite coordinate sums and apply these same comparisons. The Riesz isometry identifies the curried Hessian with the Euclidean matrix operator and preserves its norm.
